messages.text: What are the main findings of this paper?

messages.short_answer: The paper reports that its 10 non-expert participants explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically, and struggled to make robust progress. Their difficulties resembled known problems in end-user programming and interactive machine learning, and were driven by human-to-human expectations and a tendency to overgeneralize.

sections.text: The authors state that probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically. They also report that participants struggled in ways echoing end-user programming and interactive machine learning systems, and that expectations from human-to-human instruction and overgeneralization were barriers.

sections.text: According to PaperLens's summaries of the study sections, participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and rarely used error labeling or systematic testing. Participants also struggled more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and often used 'do not' phrasing even though 'do' phrasing was more effective.

sections.title: Implications the authors draw
sections.text: According to PaperLens's summaries, the authors argue that tools should support systematic testing and help users see cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversation changes. They also suggest training should clarify that instructions do not carry over between conversations, and that LLMs can be mistakenly seen as artificial general intelligence.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

These pages conclude the paper 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' and list open research questions about end-user prompt engineering, including whether societal context affects how users interact with models, whether high-context cultures struggle differently, and how tools should set capability expectations. The conclusion states that the study explored end-user intuitions and behaviors through BotDesigner, a prompt-based no-code chatbot design tool. It argues that social intuitions shape prompts, including a bias toward giving instructions over depicting examples, assumptions about capability from limited examples, and avoidance of displaying emotion. The remaining pages are acknowledgments and a reference list covering prompting, probes, and language model work.

sources.text: These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. 2.2 Known Challenges in Prompt Design While prompting can appear as easy as instructing a human, crafting efective and generalizable prompt strategies is a challenging task. How a prompt or a prompt strategy directly impacts model outputs, and how prompts modify LLMs’ billions of parameters during re-training, are both active areas of NLP research [30, 42]. Moreover, established prompt design workfows do not yet exist. Even for NLP experts, prompt engineering requires extensive trial and error, iteratively experimenting and assessing the efects of various prompt strategies on concrete input-output pairs, before assessing them more systematically on large datasets. That said, ongoing NLP research does ofer some hints toward efective prompt design strategies. Notably, these prompt strategies are efective in improving LLMs’ performance over a range of NLP tasks and conversational contexts; it remains unclear to what extent these strategies can improve any particular conversational interactions or contexts.

This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

These pages conclude the paper 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' and list open research questions about end-user prompt engineering, including whether societal context affects how users interact with models, whether high-context cultures struggle differently, and how tools should set capability expectations. The conclusion states that the study explored end-user intuitions and behaviors through BotDesigner, a prompt-based no-code chatbot design tool. It argues that social intuitions shape prompts, including a bias toward giving instructions over depicting examples, assumptions about capability from limited examples, and avoidance of displaying emotion. The remaining pages are acknowledgments and a reference list covering prompting, probes, and language model work.

Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.
